name: Carlos Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What fills an ordinary day on your crew?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: At 43, I've got a vocational certificate, an apprenticeship and years on the electricity company's rural line crew. We replace damaged spans and connect new solar sites, and I love solving a messy fitting problem in the field. What drains me is arriving with the wrong part because an office plan missed one joint.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does work fit around home and the tools you use?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Mara keeps books for a dental clinic, and our two children are still in school. We have a mortgage and roughly three months of expenses saved, so a contracting firm is an idea in my shed, not a business yet. I use AI every day for lists and planning, but I check its work against drawings before anything goes near a live line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot the AI hype was expensive, but my small planning shortcuts still save me time. No screen can put a crossarm up in the rain, and there are damaged lines waiting every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be a little disappointed because I like trying new tools, though my wages would be steadier. The mortgage and school costs mean I cannot turn my half-formed contracting idea into a gamble yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking rural repair and solar connection shifts. Each Friday I'll use the AI checklist I already use to draft next week's material order, then check every item against our drawings before I send it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. I'd still want to prove that my tools save time, even if they do not change the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner say about the contracting idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Mara would ask whether we have six months of household costs before I buy a second truck. She is right; our savings cover about three months, and the business idea can wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where has your current AI checklist gone wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month the AI order left out the larger connector for a solar feeder. I caught it against the drawing, which is why the computer gets a draft and never the final signature. The computer gets a draft material order and never my final signature.

say: My **planning shortcuts** still help with material orders, even if the wider AI boom fades.
**Rural repairs** and solar connections still need hands on poles and careful checks on the ground.
think: Stable **lineworker wages** matter more than proving that every new tool changes the trade.
Our **three-month cushion** is too small to launch my contracting idea while we carry a mortgage.
do: **Keep** rural repair and solar connection shifts at the electricity company.
**Check** AI-drafted weekly material orders against the drawings before sending them.
feel: **Calm** about wages, with some disappointment that the tools may stay modest.
S0.quote: The computer gets a draft material order and never my final signature.
fieldNote: Carlos already uses **AI daily** and gives a concrete example of catching a missed connector.
His **business ambition** is checked by the mortgage and his partner's six-month cushion threshold.

steps.text: Keep rural repair and solar connection shifts
Check AI-drafted weekly material orders against line drawings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say software can buy and schedule the parts faster, but we still have to build and repair the electricity line. If the company frees an hour, I want it spent on checking a site, not cramming in another climb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning side of my job will change first, and some office posts may go. I think a crew member who can spot bad AI orders could be useful, but I cannot assume the company will pay extra for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll run the company's permitted AI planner beside my own notes on two solar connections and log every mismatch. If the trial works, I'll show the supervisor and ask to train new crews on checking the outputs, while keeping my line shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for colleagues in the office, but I feel some room to move myself. The danger is a rushed material list leaving us stuck halfway through a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the planner misses a crucial fitting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stop ordering through it until we found where the part count went wrong. The crew cannot invent a transformer fitting beside a muddy road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would training other crews replace your line shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want paid time for the training, and I'd keep my regular roster. An occasional teaching session would not cover our mortgage if my line hours were taken away.

say: **AI scheduling** could free time, but the company should use it to check sites properly.
**Line crews** still build and repair the power network as office planning changes.
think: The company's **office roles** look more exposed than my climbing work in this slower change.
I might help check **AI orders**, though extra duties need paid time and steady line shifts.
do: **Compare** AI plans with field notes on two solar connection jobs.
**Show** recorded mismatches to the supervisor and request paid checker training if the trial works.
feel: **Uneasy** for office colleagues and wary of rushed plans, while seeing room to adapt.
S1.quote: The crew cannot invent a transformer fitting beside a muddy road.
fieldNote: He wants to **test output** on two real jobs before proposing a new role.
His interest in teaching depends on **paid time** and keeping enough line shifts for the mortgage.
He distinguishes exposed **office planning** from slower changes to physical line repair.

steps.text: Compare AI plans with field notes on two solar connections

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mates that full thinking AI by 2028 will hit our planning and my partner's clinic bookkeeping quickly. The hands-on robots around 2031 could then take whole stretches of routine line building, which is the part that would scare me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm adaptable, but a family mortgage does not bend like a spreadsheet. Mara's accounting hours could go before my line shifts, and three months of savings would be poor cover for two uncertain wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I'd ask the electricity company whether it will fund robot testing and repair training, and Mara would ask the clinic about her workload. We'd put the contracting idea on hold, cut the planned shed extension, and save that future spend from our wages while we still can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, definitely. I can learn a machine, but I cannot learn my way out of a household losing both pay packets at once. I can learn a line-repair robot, but I cannot learn my way out of two lost pay packets at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about the cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our children the shed extension is off, and that the school costs are still in the budget. I would not tell them a robot is certain to take my job; we do not know the company's crew plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start the contracting firm before the robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a company-funded testing place if it led to a real paid roster before 2031. I would not quit to start a line contracting firm while customers might be replacing crews with robots.

say: **2028 thinking AI** could change scheduling and clinic accounts before line-repair robots arrive around 2031.
The company owes crews a **paid training path** before it buys capable robots for field jobs.
think: Mara's **clinic bookkeeping** and my later line shifts could both shrink, leaving our mortgage vulnerable.
Our **three-month savings** would not carry a long gap in two wages.
do: **Ask** both employers for staffing plans and request company-funded robot testing training.
**Cancel** the planned shed extension and cut that discretionary spending.
**Save** the wages intended for the extension while both jobs still pay.
feel: **Anxious** by the chance of losing two household incomes in a short span.
S2.quote: I can learn a line-repair robot, but I cannot learn my way out of two lost pay packets at once.
fieldNote: Daily AI use does not erase his **household exposure** through clinic bookkeeping and a mortgage.
He delays the **contracting plan** because clients may also switch to robots.
Training is conditional on a **company-funded place** and a paid roster.

steps.text: Take company-funded robot testing training if it leads to a paid roster
Cancel planned shed extension and cut discretionary spending
Save extension budget from wages while both jobs still pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the five-year picture gives us room to trial robots on easy sections before a full field rollout around 2034. Thinking AI in 2031 would sort the work orders sooner, so the company should show us what it expects of crews at both dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By then I could be the person who tests machines on awkward rural spans, if that paid role exists. I also know how fast an interesting pilot can turn into fewer ordinary line shifts for everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll ask to join a supervised robot inspection trial and keep a notebook of failures in wind, mud and tight clearances. Mara and I will set an extra monthly mortgage payment from my regular wages, but only while her clinic hours hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the runway gives me a job to do now. I'd rather bring the supervisor a page of field failures than a speech about progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a robot trial convincing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make them repeat the test in the same mud and wind with a crew ready to stop it. A sunny demonstration behind a fence would not tell me whether it can repair a country line. A sunny robot demonstration behind a fence won't repair a country power line in mud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your partner's clinic hours fall first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the clinic reduces Mara's hours, the extra mortgage payment stops that month. We would cover the ordinary bills before paying debt ahead of schedule.

say: **Supervised trials** on difficult rural spans matter more than polished demonstrations before the 2034 robot date.
The electricity company should explain **crew numbers** for both the 2031 thinking shift and later field robots.
think: A paid **robot-testing role** might suit me, but no one has promised such a vacancy.
Pilots can still reduce **ordinary line shifts** even when one worker gains a specialist role.
do: **Join** a supervised inspection trial if the electricity company offers one.
**Record** robot failures in wind, mud and tight clearances.
**Overpay** the mortgage monthly from regular wages only while clinic hours hold.
feel: **Anxious** about crew hours, with useful time to test and prepare.
S3.quote: A sunny robot demonstration behind a fence won't repair a country power line in mud.
fieldNote: He proposes **field trials** under conditions that make rural linework difficult.
His mortgage overpayment is **conditional** on Mara retaining clinic hours.
He sees a possible **specialist role** but does not assume a vacancy or protected crew size.

steps.text: Join supervised robot inspection trial and record rural-site failures
Overpay mortgage monthly only while Mara retains clinic hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew ten years is long enough to choose what we want to build alongside the machines. Thinking AI arrives in 2036 and field robots around 2039; I want the company to offer real inspection jobs, not just a farewell lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 56 around the robot date, and my children will be older. A small contracting shop might still make sense for unusual repairs, but only if there are customers and we have paid down the mortgage; robots might erase that market too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my line certificate current, learn the company's new testing equipment as it arrives, and ask for annual numbers on paid inspection openings. Each year Mara and I will review the mortgage and school costs before deciding whether to fund a small contracting business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful than in the fast pictures. Having choices is good, even when I cannot say which choice will pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you steer your children into linework?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show them what a real line apprenticeship involves and let them pick their own work. I wouldn't tell my children to join my trade just because I enjoyed it; by 2039 the entry jobs may be different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make your contracting shop real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want an actual customer order for difficult line repairs and six months of family expenses in cash first. Without both, the workshop stays a shed, not a company. Without a customer order and six months of family expenses, my line-repair workshop stays a shed, not a company.

say: A **decade** allows the electricity company to train crews for inspections before field robots arrive around 2039.
A **real inspection job** needs pay and a roster, not a ceremonial title.
think: At **56**, I might have a viable repair business, but robot competition could remove those customers.
I want my **children** to choose work based on the jobs that actually exist when they leave school.
do: **Renew** the linework certificate and learn company testing equipment as it arrives.
**Ask** annually for numbers of paid inspection openings.
**Review** mortgage and school costs each year before funding any repair shop.
feel: **Uneasy** about the market, but hopeful about having time to choose.
S4.quote: Without a customer order and six months of family expenses, my line-repair workshop stays a shed, not a company.
fieldNote: He retains a **business ambition**, but sets two conditions before putting family money into it.
He asks for actual **paid inspection vacancies** rather than assuming retraining guarantees one.
His children's **future choices** matter more than preserving his own trade for them.

steps.text: Renew linework certificate and keep working on rural lines
Wait for customers and six months savings before funding repair shop

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because Mara's clinic accounting could change quickly and robots might cut my line shifts around 2031. A published crew plan and a company-paid testing place with actual wages would help us decide whether to stay or look elsewhere.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays when a clever machine orders the wrong fitting and sends a crew home. A screen can make a plan in a minute, but the family mortgage comes due every month. I won't gamble our house on a tool being right most of the time. I won't gamble our house on a planning tool being right most of the time.

headlineQuote: I won't gamble our house on a planning tool being right most of the time.
portrait: **Carlos**, 43, repairs rural electricity lines and connects solar sites after a vocational certificate and apprenticeship.
He uses **AI daily** for planning, yet catches wrong material orders by checking them against drawings.
A **mortgage**, two school-age children and three months of savings limit his wish to start a line-repair business.
He would test robots in **real field conditions** and wants paid inspection work before ordinary crew shifts shrink.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could reduce his partner's clinic accounting hours before robots threaten his line shifts around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A published **crew plan** and company-paid robot testing place with real wages would help him decide his next move.
